title: Who a Fractional CFO Reports To, and What They Decide
summary: Fractional CFO decision rights decide whether the work lands. See who the role reports to, what it owns, and how it fits beside your controller or bookkeeper.
body_markdown:
## Who a Fractional CFO Reports To


Fractional CFO decision rights are what owners are really asking about when they wonder where this person would even sit. In a business with no finance executive, you’ve been doing the job already. In the evening, between customer calls, on a spreadsheet nobody else opens. So the reporting line isn’t an org-chart detail. It’s a handoff, and indinero’s[CFO Services](https://www.indinero.com/services/cfo-services/) treat naming it as the first piece of work rather than a prerequisite.


Most owners arrive here asking who does a fractional CFO report to. The answer is short. The owner or CEO, as a direct report, with no layer in between. That isn’t a preference. The job was already being held by the person at the top, and a direct line is the only structure that finishes the handoff.


Reporting lines are a control question, not an aesthetic one.[COSO’s Internal Control Integrated Framework](https://www.coso.org/guidance-on-ic) puts structures, reporting lines, and appropriate authorities and responsibilities inside the control environment, the foundation management establishes with board oversight. Vague lines create gaps. If two people each assume the other reviews the forecast assumptions, nobody reviews the forecast assumptions.


The National Association of Corporate Directors makes the same point about authority. Its[director essentials on board and management roles](https://www.nacdonline.org/all-governance/governance-resources/governance-research/director-faqs-and-essentials/role-board-vs-role-management/) states that “clear, documented delegation of authority strengthens accountability,” and that boards and management should revisit delegated authority as leadership, strategy, and conditions change. Adding strategic financial leadership to a business that has never had any is exactly that kind of change.


Where the line lands depends on what already sits above it.


- **Single owner, no leadership team.** The CFO reports to you, on a fixed cadence, same day and same agenda. The risk is isolation. You become the only person who sees the analysis, and the business gets a smarter owner instead of a better-run company.
- **A leadership team already exists.** The CFO still reports to the owner or CEO and sits beside the function heads, not above them. No dotted lines into sales or operations. Bringing a fractional CFO into the leadership team becomes a literal act here, a standing seat and a standing agenda slot instead of a guest appearance when something is wrong.
- **Two or more owners.** Name the line out loud, and name it to one person. Either one owner is the line and the other is informed, or both are the line with a stated tiebreak. Left unnamed, the analysis stops being analysis and starts being ammunition.
- **A board or advisory board exists.** The CFO reports to management and presents to the board. Presenting is not reporting. A fractional CFO reporting line that runs solid to the board turns the role into an agent of oversight, and you lose a partner.


Boards are hungry for what this role produces. NACD’s[2024 Private Company Board Practices and Oversight Survey](https://www.nacdonline.org/all-governance/governance-resources/governance-surveys/surveys-benchmarking/2024-private-company-board-practices-and-oversight-survey/board-reporting/) , fielded to 214 private company directors and advisers, found 45 percent saying board materials emphasize operational matters over strategy. That’s the gap you feel when the monthly package says what happened and nothing about what to do.


So write down two lines. Who the CFO reports to, by name, and who they escalate to when that person is unreachable for a week. If you’re still weighing whether the business is ready, readiness here is operational complexity rather than a revenue figure, and our[stage guide on when to hire a CFO](https://www.indinero.com/blog/when-to-hire-a-cfo-stage-guide/) works through the signals.


## What the Role Decides and What It Only Advises


A fractional CFO decides the method. You decide the commitment. That one line resolves most of the friction a new finance voice creates, and it’s worth settling before anybody builds a forecast.


The role owns the forecast, the analysis, the recommendation on record, the reporting standard, and the sequence of finance improvements. You keep capital, hiring, pricing, and every commitment that carries a signature.


Area The fractional CFO decides You and your leadership team decide


Forecast Model structure, the drivers, scenario ranges, and the method for rolling it forward The commercial assumptions that reflect intent, such as a planned price move


Reporting standard Which measures appear in the management package, how each is defined, and the cadence Whether to add a measure you want to see


Analysis and recommendation The recommendation on record, including the one leadership declines Whether to accept it


Finance roadmap The sequence of improvements, what gets fixed first in the close, the chart of accounts Anything in that sequence that needs spend or a new hire


Capital allocation and CapEx The model, the ranking, the payback and return on investment case The allocation itself


Pricing Margin analysis, unit economics, the recommended structure, and discount guardrails List price, discount policy, and what to tell a specific customer


Hiring and headcount The cost, the timing, and the payback case for a role The hire


Working capital Targets and mechanics, days sales outstanding goals, collection cadence, inventory turnover targets Whether to accept a term that hurts cash to win an account


Covenant monitoring and lender reporting The reporting a lender requires, the covenant headroom model, and the early warning Signing anything


Payment release and bank authorization Nothing. The role reviews the payment run, never releases it You keep this


Those last two rows are structural, not a trust judgment. Owners get this wrong in the friendliest possible way. They like the CFO, so they hand over the bank.


Internal-control guidance from state comptroller and inspector general offices keeps three duties apart: custody of assets, authorization of the transactions affecting them, and recording those transactions. Where separating all three isn’t practical, the guidance calls for compensating controls. A CFO who recommends a spend and also releases the payment holds authorization and custody at once, which makes every later recommendation look self-interested. The workable arrangements for a small team sit in our guide to[segregation of duties on a small finance team](https://www.indinero.com/blog/segregation-of-duties-small-finance-team/) .


Fractional CFO authority doesn’t come from the title either. A 2024 study of the CFO role published by AICPA and CIMA, conducted by Professor Paul Thambar of Monash University, is built from in-depth interviews with 12 CFOs ([A study of role expectations, conflicts and ambiguity](https://www.aicpa-cima.com/professional-insights/download/the-chief-financial-officer-cfo-a-study-of-role-expectations-conflicts-and-ambiguity) ). That makes it a qualitative role finding, not a population statistic, and what it names is useful. The CFOs interviewed managed conflicting expectations by building trust and working relationships, not by invoking the org chart.


Influence gets earned through the quality of the questions in the first few months. Which argues for a clear decision lane over a big title. One standing rule makes the lane work. The CFO should be able to put “I recommend against this” in writing, in a form that outlives the meeting. The decision stays yours. The record is the point, because the useful question six months later isn’t who was right. It’s whether the business can see why it chose what it chose.


## How the Role Sits Beside Your Controller or Bookkeeper


A CFO who uses the numbers is not the same as a controller who produces them, and one person rarely does both well at once. Your bookkeeper or controller is the steward of accurate, timely reporting. The CFO is the strategist who reads those reports and shapes what the business does next. If you’re still deciding which of those roles you need, that question has its own answer and we keep it there on purpose. Start with[which finance role your business actually needs](https://www.indinero.com/blog/controller-vs-comptroller-vs-cfo/) , and see the steward side of the work in[outsourced controller services](https://www.indinero.com/blog/outsourced-controller-services/) .


What matters on this page is the working relationship, and it runs in two directions.


- **Up to the CFO.** The ledger, the close, the trial balance, the reconciliations, the supporting detail. The role is a consumer of the close.
- **Down from the CFO.** Questions, variance follow-ups, and a standard the close has to meet. The role is a specifier of the close, never a producer of it.


The second direction is where the tension lives. Three arrangements are workable, and none of them is permanent.


**An advisory relationship.** The bookkeeper’s solid line stays where it is, often to you or an office manager. The CFO carries no management authority, only a working relationship and a right to ask. That’s the right starting point for most businesses, because the team absorbs nothing on day one.


**A dotted line to the CFO.** The solid line stays internal, and the CFO sets the reporting standard, reviews judgment items, and becomes the person your bookkeeper takes a hard question to. Most engagements land here after a few months, usually by use rather than by announcement.


**A solid line to the CFO.** Appropriate once you’ve decided the finance function needs to be led rather than supervised. Treat that as a deliberate choice about how the finance team gets built, not an automatic consequence of bringing a CFO in.


One failure mode deserves naming, because nobody warns owners about it. If the CFO starts posting entries, chasing a reconciliation, or living in the accounting system all month, the engagement has quietly become a bookkeeping engagement. The forecast goes stale, and you conclude that CFO leadership didn’t work when it never got to start.


If the CFO closes the books, there is no CFO.


Five handoff points prevent most of that, and none of them takes a document:


1. The close date. One date, fixed, the same every month.
2. Who answers variance questions, and in what form.
3. Where chart of accounts change requests go, and who approves a new general ledger account.
4. Who performs each reconciliation, and who reviews it.
5. Who your bookkeeper escalates to when a CFO request collides with existing workload.


The role tension those AICPA and CIMA interviews describe, steward against business partner, shows up inside a small finance team too. Hold one person to both the production standard and the strategic standard and production wins, because production has a deadline. That isn’t a character flaw. It’s structure.


## Preparing Your Team for a New Voice in the Numbers


Your bookkeeper will hear “we’re bringing in a CFO” as an audit of their work unless you say otherwise first, in person, before the CFO arrives.


Here’s how it goes when you don’t. You send a short note to the team on a Thursday. By Friday your bookkeeper has quietly pulled three years of reconciliations, re-checked a write-off from 2023, and started wondering whether to update a resume. Nothing in the note mentioned performance.


It didn’t have to.


The sequence that works is short, and the order matters more than the wording.


1. **Tell your finance person first.** Before the team announcement, not the same day.
2. **Name complexity as the reason, not performance.** More entities, more locations, a lender, a decision the business can’t make on instinct anymore. The business outgrew the structure, which is a compliment to whoever held it together this long.
3. **Say what is not changing.** Their job, their reporting line, their responsibilities. Say it in those words, because the absence of that sentence is what people fill in with fear.
4. **Name what will change, concretely.** The specifics below are far less frightening than the imagination.
5. **Give them something they wanted.** Most bookkeepers in a growing business have an improvement they’ve been asking for and losing. A CFO is the person who will now argue for it with you.


### What actually changes in their month


**A close deadline that holds.** APQC’s open standards benchmarking data on general accounting, reported in[CFO.com’s metric of the month on close cycle time](https://www.cfo.com/news/metric-of-the-month-cycle-time-for-monthly-close/659297/) , puts the median at 6.4 calendar days to complete monthly consolidated financial statements, with the top quartile at 4.8 days or less and the bottom quartile at 10 or more, across more than 2,300 organizations. Nobody is asking for heroics in month one. The ask is a date that holds, because analysis on day 18 is history and analysis on day 7 is a decision.


**A cleaner chart of accounts.** The same analysis found that organizations with widespread adoption of a standard chart of accounts shave roughly two days off the close compared with low adopters. Restructuring the chart of accounts is often a CFO’s first request, and it reads as criticism when it’s actually the highest-return single change available.


**Requests for detail nobody has asked for before.** Revenue by customer and by product or service line. Margin by job or project. Receivables aging with payment behavior rather than buckets. Inventory by turn. Payroll by department. Much of it already exists in the system and has simply never been pulled, which is worth telling someone who assumes the request means their work was incomplete.


**Work moving earlier in the month.** Recurring entries and reconciliations shifting ahead of period end, so the close becomes a review instead of a scramble. That reshapes the month more than the deadline does.


**A written close procedure.** Documented steps, owners, and dates. Not bureaucracy. Insurance against the business depending on one person’s memory.


### What your leadership team should expect to be asked for


Owners prepare the bookkeeper and forget everyone else. A CFO’s inputs come from operations as much as from the ledger, and they land better when people know they’re coming.


- **Sales.** Pipeline with dates and probability, actual discount given against list, customer concentration, and the terms being offered to win deals.
- **Operations.** Capacity, utilization, rework or scrap, lead times, and a hiring plan with start dates rather than a count.
- **Service or delivery.** Units or hours delivered against units or hours billed, which is where margin usually leaks.
- **Anyone asking for money.** A return and payback case, not just a request.
- **Everyone.** One standing agenda slot for the numbers in the leadership meeting, in the same place each month, whether or not anything is wrong. What belongs in that slot is a reporting decision, and our guide to[KPI dashboards for business leaders](https://www.indinero.com/blog/kpi-dashboards-for-business-leaders/) covers how to hold it to the measures that matter.


Set the expectation on timing too. The first two closes under a new reporting standard are noisy. The third is useful. Saying that at the start keeps anyone from judging the engagement on month one, and keeps your bookkeeper from carrying blame for noise a change in standard always produces.


## How Indinero Fits CFO Leadership Into an Existing Team


Indinero keeps CFO leadership strategic and distinct. The role uses the numbers. Our accounting team produces them. Accounting and tax work stays coordinated with the CFO work rather than folded into it, because the moment the strategist also owns the production, the strategy stops happening.


Indinero has operated continuously since 2009 and supports 500+ regular customers, which matters here for one narrow reason. The structural question this page is about, where the role sits and what it’s allowed to decide, is one we’ve worked through inside hundreds of teams that already had a bookkeeper or a controller in place.


The work itself is organized around four themes, and the reporting and authority angle runs through each one.


- **See Clearly.** Profitability analysis and margin improvement, KPI development, and management and leadership reporting. This is where the role’s decision right over the reporting standard turns into something your leadership team can actually see.
- **Plan Forward.** Rolling forecasts, cash flow and working capital management, and growth and scenario planning, maintained continuously rather than run as a project. The role owns the method and the model. You own the commercial assumptions inside it.
- **Decide Well.** Decision support and financial modeling, capital allocation and CapEx strategy, pricing strategy, and interim CFO leadership. Event-driven, one decision at a time. This is where the advise-and-decide line is most visible, because each piece of work ends in a recommendation and you make the call.
- **Build Value.** Process improvement, working capital optimization, finance function and team development, and the multi-year work of building enterprise value.


That last theme is the answer to this page’s question. Defining the boundaries between bookkeeping, controller oversight, and CFO leadership, and getting to a right-sized finance structure, is part of the Build Value work itself. You don’t have to settle the reporting line, the decision rights, and the team structure before CFO leadership can start.


So an owner stuck on “I don’t know where this person would sit” isn’t unprepared. They’re describing the first piece of work.


A few things stay true in every structure we’ve worked inside. Your existing bookkeeper keeps their job, and keeping them is the normal outcome rather than the exception. If there’s already a controller, the CFO sits beside that person and above the reporting standard, not on top of the individual. Readiness is operational complexity, meaning multiple entities or locations, inventory or job costing, a lender relationship, a second owner, or a leadership team that disagrees about where the money should go.


Not a revenue figure.


If that sounds like your business, the next useful conversation isn’t about scope. It’s about structure, and about what CFO leadership would and wouldn’t take off your desk. That’s usually where[our CFO Services](https://www.indinero.com/services/cfo-services/) start.


## Frequently asked questions


Most of what owners ask next sits on the edges of the role. Signing authority, meeting attendance, how to introduce the role to the person who currently handles your books, and what a CFO actually needs to see. The same rule runs through all of it. The role decides the method, and you decide the commitment.


### Does a fractional CFO have signing authority?


Normally a fractional CFO has no signing authority, because the owner or a designated officer keeps release authority while the role recommends and reviews. That’s a control decision, not a trust judgment. Internal control guidance separates custody of assets, authorization of transactions, and recording of transactions, and a CFO who builds the forecast and also releases payments collapses two of those. Where a small team can’t separate all three cleanly, compensating controls cover the gap.


### Should a fractional CFO attend our leadership meetings?


Yes, a fractional CFO should sit in the leadership sessions where decisions with financial consequences actually get made. The value is hearing the operating conversation directly rather than reading a summary of it a week later, because margin pressure, a pricing concession, a hire, or a term that delays cash all surface in the room before they reach the ledger. A CFO who only appears in a crisis is read as a crisis.


### How do we introduce a fractional CFO to our bookkeeper?


Tell your bookkeeper about the fractional CFO first, in person, before the team announcement, and name complexity as the reason rather than performance. Say plainly what isn’t changing, their job, their reporting line, their responsibilities, and say that a CFO uses the numbers rather than producing them. Then name what actually changes in their month, a firmer close deadline, a cleaner chart of accounts, and requests for detail nobody has asked them for before.


### Can a fractional CFO manage our in-house finance staff?


A fractional CFO usually provides functional oversight rather than line management, because employment and performance authority stay with the business. The CFO sets the reporting standard and reviews the work, and you hold the employment relationship, so moving the solid line to the CFO is a deliberate choice rather than an automatic consequence of bringing the role in. At indinero, defining those boundaries is part of the CFO work itself rather than something you settle beforehand.


### What financial decisions should still sit with the owner?


Capital allocation, hiring, pricing, owner compensation, payment release, and any signature stay with the owner, not with the fractional CFO. The CFO owns the forecast, the analysis, the recommendation on record, the reporting standard, and the sequence of finance improvements. That split is a feature rather than a limit, because the person who carries the consequence of a commitment should be the one making it. A good CFO wants it that way.


### What access does a fractional CFO actually need?


A fractional CFO needs read access to the accounting system and bank data, the historical close, the chart of accounts, contracts, and payroll detail. Contracts and terms matter more than owners expect, because they govern when cash actually arrives rather than when revenue gets recorded. Read access is the default, and the role shouldn’t need the ability to post entries, initiate payments, change vendor banking details, or add users.
